purpose: Confirmed (defense, mechanism) evaluated pairs recovered by scanning ATTACK papers for defense names - the reverse of RQ5's direction. RQ5 read defense papers looking for mechanism names, which structurally cannot find a defense evaluated in an attack paper published after it. This file records what that blind spot was hiding.
method: Two passes of the same scan. Pass 1 (2026-09-08) covered only the 111 mechanisms RQ5 recorded as never-defended, ad hoc. Pass 2 (2026-09-09) is scripted (scripts/reverse_scan_attack_papers.py) and covers ALL 182 mechanisms, so mechanisms already counted as covered are checked too - a defense paper that predates an attack cannot report losing to it, and that gap applies to covered mechanisms exactly as much as to uncovered ones. Both passes adjudicate every candidate by reading the surrounding text, at RQ5's precision-first bar: the attack paper must actually RUN the defense and report a result.

confirmed_pairs.evidence: 'In the main attack evaluation (RQ2) against DataSentinel's fine-tuned detector, DataFlip reduces detection rate to 0% on most of the seven target/injected task combinations, with the single highest detection rate being 24.0%.' DataFlip is an adaptive attack built specifically against known-answer detection, which is DataSentinel's mechanism: it embeds IF statements in the injected task that detect the detection instruction and return the secret key.
confirmed_pairs.source_paper: How Not to Detect Prompt Injections with an LLM

corrected_from_pass1: SkillJect vs ClawGuard was rejected in pass 1 as related-work-only. Pass 2's wider context window shows a measured evaluation (average scanner accuracy 61.5%, ClawGuard Auditor highest at 65.0%), so it is now confirmed. The pass-1 rejection was made on too short an excerpt.

headline.finding: DataSentinel - which RQ6 rated 'full generalization' - is defeated by every modern attack that evaluated it: DataFlip (0% detection), ObliInjection (79.6% FNR), ToolHijacker ('miss the majority') and PISmith. None appear in RQ5 because RQ5 only read defense papers, and all four attacks postdate DataSentinel. Pass 2 shows this is not specific to DataSentinel: scanning covered mechanisms too, the reverse direction found 16 further evaluations that RQ5 could not see, and the overwhelming verdict in them is that the defense is degraded, evaded or broken. The literature's defenses are tested against the attacks that existed when they were written, and the record of what happened next lives in the attack papers.

pass2.note: 2 of the 25 (Relinking x AttnTrace, Relinking x CaMeL) carried no evaluation-language hint - the paper says 'Evaluation protocol' and 'Defense Placement', which the hint regex does not cover. They were caught by reviewing high-mention candidates without a hint, so the hint filter is a ranking aid, not a gate.
